title: Decision tree for edit distance
summary: Modeling strings as nodes and single edits as directed edges frames the problem as finding the shortest path from hello to algo in a decision tree; the figure expands one three-step transformation path while leaving other branches unexpanded.
context: In the decision tree model, each node represents a string state, and each outgoing directed edge represents one decision (a single insertion, deletion, or replacement operation). Finding the edit distance from string s = hello to t = algo is equivalent to finding the shortest path from the root node hello to the target node algo in this decision tree.
description: From top to bottom on the left, the figure expands a single path of 4 string nodes and 3 directed edges, starting from s = hello at the top and ending at t = algo at the bottom. The table below lists each edge and its operation in order; the first edge in the drawing reads only "Replace l with g," and "the second l" is added by comparing the two node strings to clarify the position.

To the right of each expanded node in the top three levels (hello, helgo, and halgo), 3 additional branch arrows point to ellipses "...", indicating that without restrictions on edits, every string can branch into many other edit choices; those abbreviated branches omit specific strings, since the figure illustrates the shortest-path perspective on the decision tree rather than exhausting the entire search tree.

frames.title: Three-step edit path from hello to algo
frames.explanation: This path reaches algo from hello in 3 edits, matching the edit distance of 3 shown in Figure 14-27 earlier in this section. Examining this single expanded path only confirms that 3 edits suffice; by itself, it cannot rule out a shorter path.
